title: AI at school: help or shortcut?
essentialQuestion: When does an AI tool help you learn, and when does it get in the way?
learningGoal: Explain how AI chat tools can help or harm learning, and suggest fair rules for a school.

warmUp.question: Which use of an AI tool helps a student learn more?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which student used the helper to learn? Which student used it as a shortcut?

cards.title: Three students and the Brightwater homework helper (a pretend tool)

cases.name: Mira
cases.body: Mira does not understand fractions. She asks the helper to explain them in a different way, with an example about sharing bread. Then she does the practice questions herself.

cases.name: Jonah
cases.body: Jonah asks the helper to write his whole essay about rivers. He hands it in as his own work. The next day, he can't answer his teacher's questions about it.

cases.name: Ayla
cases.body: Ayla asks the helper to translate a science page into a language she reads well. One word looks strange, so she checks it with her teacher.

cards.title: Brightwater School's draft rules for the homework helper
items: Ask for a hint before you ask for an answer.
Say when you used the helper, and what for.
Check facts in a book or with a teacher.
Never type your name, address or other private information.
Everyone can use the helper on the school's laptops, not only students with their own phone.

activity.title: Try the pretend helper
activity.toolLabel: Pretend tool. Its answers were written in advance for this lesson. It is not a real AI, and nothing you choose is sent anywhere.
activity.instructions: First, choose the request that would help Jonah learn. Then check an answer from the tool.

start.prompt: Write my answer: why do many towns grow near rivers?
start.answer: Many towns grow near rivers because rivers give people water, food and a way to travel. Here is your finished answer. You can hand it in.

improve.question: Which request would help Jonah learn the most?

options.prompt: Write a longer answer for me.
options.answer: Many towns grow near rivers. Rivers give water for drinking and farming. They give fish to eat. Boats can carry people and goods. Here is your longer answer.
options.feedback: Not quite. A longer answer is still the tool's work. Jonah does not have to think.

options.prompt: Give me a hint. Then let me try first.
options.answer: Hint: think about what people need every day. What can a river give them? Write your idea. Then I will ask you a question about it.
options.feedback: Yes. A hint helps Jonah think. He still does the learning himself.

options.prompt: Change the words so it looks like mine.
options.answer: Here is the same answer in new words. Towns often start beside rivers, because rivers bring water, food and travel.
options.feedback: Not quite. This hides who did the work. That is not honest, and Jonah learns nothing new.

check.prompt: When was the old bridge in Brightwater built?
check.answer: The old bridge in Brightwater was built in 1850. I am completely sure about this.

trustedSource.name: The Brightwater town history book
trustedSource.says: The old bridge was built in 1920. Before that, people crossed the river by boat.

check.question: The tool sounds very sure. What should you do?

options.text: Trust it, because it sounds sure
options.feedback: Not quite. A tool can sound sure and still be wrong. Check a trusted source.

options.text: Ask the tool to say it again
options.feedback: Not quite. The tool may give the same wrong answer. Check a different source.
Yes. The book says 1920. The tool made up a date, even though it sounded sure.

activity.saves: The learner's choices, with the lesson's other answers. Nothing is typed into a real tool.
activity.offline: Every request and answer is written in the lesson file. No AI model runs, and nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: Schools are deciding how to use AI
sections.text: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. Many people use them, including many students. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use these tools? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had rules or formal guidance about AI tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for countries. It said they should protect students' privacy, and set an age limit, such as 13, for children using these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not a law, and it is not about every learning tool.
sections.simpler: AI chat tools can answer questions and even write essays. Schools must decide how to use them. In 2023, UNESCO asked over 450 schools and universities. UNESCO is the United Nations group for education. Fewer than 1 in 10 had guidance about AI. Then UNESCO wrote guidance for countries. Protect students' privacy, it said. Set an age, like 13, for children to chat with AI alone. This is advice, not a law.

sections.heading: A tool can help you learn
sections.text: Used well, an AI tool can work a bit like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in simpler words, give you extra practice or translate a page into a language you know. At the made-up Brightwater School, Mira asks the homework helper to explain fractions in a new way. Then she does the practice herself. In 2024, researchers tested an AI tutor for English with secondary school students in Nigeria. For six weeks, students used it after school, and trained teachers guided every session. On English tests at the end, they did better than students who did not take part.
sections.simpler: An AI tool can be a bit like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in easy words, or give you more practice. At Brightwater School, Mira asks the helper about fractions. Then she does the practice herself. In 2024, students in Nigeria used an AI tutor after school for six weeks. Teachers guided them. They did better on English tests than other students.

sections.heading: A tool can also be a shortcut
sections.text: An AI tool can also become a shortcut that gets in the way. In a study in Türkiye, nearly 1,000 high school students practised maths. Some used a chat tool that gave full answers. They did better in practice, but worse on a test without the tool. Students whose tool gave hints, written with teachers' help, did about as well as students with no tool. Each study was one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ. A tool can also be wrong and still sound sure, and not every student has a device. So Brightwater's draft rules ask for hints first, honest work and checks with a teacher.
sections.simpler: A tool can also be a shortcut. Then you learn less. In one study, nearly 1,000 students practised maths. Some had a tool that gave full answers. They did well in practice. On a test with no tool, they did worse. Others had a tool that gave hints, made with teachers. They did as well as students without one. Results may differ in other places. A tool can be wrong but sound sure. Not everyone has a device. Brightwater's rules say: hints first, honest work, and check with a teacher.

glossary.definition: Advice from a group about how something should be done.
glossary.example: UNESCO wrote guidance about AI tools in schools.

glossary.definition: Keeping your own information safe from people who should not see it.
glossary.example: Brightwater's rules protect privacy: never type your address into the helper.

glossary.definition: A person who helps one student, or a few, learn something.
glossary.example: The helper explained fractions to Mira, a bit like a tutor.

glossary.definition: A quicker way that skips some of the steps.
glossary.example: Jonah used the helper as a shortcut, so he learned nothing about rivers.

glossary.definition: Telling the truth, including about who did the work.
glossary.example: An honest student says when they used the helper.

checks.question: In the maths study in Türkiye, what happened when the tool gave full answers?

options.text: They did best of all on the test
options.feedback: Not quite. They did well in practice, but not on the test. Read the third section.

options.text: They did worse on the test
options.feedback: Yes. The tool did the work in practice. On a test without it, they did worse.
Not quite. They used it a lot in practice. Read the third section again.

checks.question: Which rule would help students learn the most?

options.feedback: Not quite. Then the tool does the thinking. Look at Brightwater's draft rules.

options.text: Only the fastest students may use it
options.feedback: Not quite. That is not fair, and it does not help anyone learn. Look at the rules again.

options.text: Ask for a hint before an answer
options.feedback: Yes. A hint helps you think, so you still do the learning yourself.

checks.question: Which Brightwater rule do you think matters most? Why?
checks.placeholder: The rule that matters most is ... because ...

write.prompt: Brightwater School wants help with its rules for the homework helper. Write two rules, and explain how each one helps students learn or keeps things fair.
selfCheck: I wrote two rules for Brightwater School.
I explained how each rule helps students learn or keeps things fair.
I used evidence from the lesson.
write.example: My first rule is: ask for a hint before you ask for an answer. This rule helps because students still do the thinking. In the lesson, the study in Türkiye shows that students who got full answers did worse on a test without the tool. My second rule is: everyone can use the helper on the school laptops. This is fair because not every student has a phone at home. Ayla used it to translate a page, and then she checked a word with her teacher.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner names one way a student could use the homework helper. You say “help” or “shortcut” and give one reason. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud one way an AI tool can help learning, one way it can get in the way, and one rule you would make.

watch.title: What are AI Chatbots?
watch.why: This short cartoon explains why AI chat tools are made to sound like people, which can make their answers feel more true than they are.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why do you think an AI chat tool can sound like a real person?
watch.afterQuestion: Why should a student check what a chat tool says, even when it sounds sure?
watch.summary: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work. It also asks why many of them are made to sound like people. A chatbot can sound friendly and human. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel. And check what it says before you trust it.
keyPoints: Many AI chatbots are made to sound like people.
Sounding human and sure does not make an answer true.
Notice how a chatbot makes you feel, and check what it says.
watch.contentNote: An American cartoon, 3 minutes 20 seconds (as listed on Common Sense Education's video page). The title and channel were checked with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026. The summary was written from Common Sense Education's description of the video (why chatbots are designed to sound so human-like, and how that might affect us) and the aims of the lesson that uses it, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it and check the summary before use. Learners can read the written summary instead.

UNESCO (7 September 2023): Governments must quickly regulate generative AI in schools (press release, age limit of 13; GCED Clearinghouse copy)
UNESCO (2023): Survey, less than 10% of schools and universities have formal guidance on AI (GCED Clearinghouse copy)
World Bank (May 2025): From chalkboards to chatbots, evaluating the impact of generative AI on learning outcomes in Nigeria (De Simone and others, Policy Research Working Paper 11125)

Bastani and others (PNAS, 2025): Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, evidence from high school mathematics (record; reported by Knowledge at Wharton, August 2024, for the study in Türkiye)

sensitiveNotes: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks countries to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools (its press release names 13); it is guidance, not a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline. UNESCO's wording differs between sources: its catalogue record says the guidance proposes "setting an age limit for independent conversations with GenAI platforms"; its press release says it "sets an age limit of 13 for the use of AI tools in the classroom". The lesson says it suggests an age such as 13 for using chat tools alone. The full guidance couldn't be opened in this revision: check it before teaching.
Some learners have no device or internet where they live. Talk about access as a fairness question for schools, never as something to compare between learners.
educatorNotes: The Brightwater students, the pretend tool's answers and the 1850 bridge date are made up; the wrong date is written on purpose so learners practise checking. Paper version of the activity: read the requests and answers aloud and let learners choose.

The two studies, simplified (see sources and claims/DW11.md). Nigeria: a World Bank randomised trial in public senior secondary schools in Edo State (Benin City), June to July 2024: six weeks of after-school English sessions, twice a week, with a large language model and teachers trained to guide each session; on a pen-and-paper test of English, AI knowledge and digital skills, gains were about 0.3 standard deviations (0.23 to 0.24 on English), and students also did better on end-of-year exams. The authors can't separate the AI from the teacher support and prompts, and don't know if it lasts or works in other subjects or ordinary classes. Türkiye: Bastani and others (PNAS, 2025): nearly 1,000 high school maths students; with GPT-4 during practice, the plain chat tool raised practice grades by 48% but lowered grades on a later exam without AI by 17%; the hint-giving tutor, with teacher input, raised practice grades by 127% and left exam grades about the same as no AI. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
changes: Replaces the draft “Asking an AI tool good questions” (October 2026, social studies rebuild), now retired/DW08-asking-good-questions.json. The lesson moves from prompting skills to a social studies question: how schools and families decide about AI tools, who benefits, and what the risks are.

Keeps the ask-tool activity (a labelled pretend tool with pre-written answers, including a sure-but-wrong answer to check against a book), reframed around learning rather than better prompts, and reuses its video, Common Sense Education's “What are AI Chatbots?”.

New real evidence: UNESCO's 2023 survey and guidance, a study in Türkiye and a 2024 pilot in Nigeria. Learner text names UNESCO and the two countries but no researchers or companies; check this fits spec section 5.3 for the social studies rebuild.
The Write task asks for rules for a made-up school, not about learners' own use of AI.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: kept the pretend tool and activity. Cited both studies with who, what and how (Nigeria: secondary school students, English, six weeks after school with trained teachers guiding, tested at the end; Türkiye: nearly 1,000 high school maths students, full answers versus hints written with teachers, practice versus a test without the tool) and said each was one subject in one place, in both readings. UNESCO's 2023 age guidance is now described as advice about children using chat tools on their own, not a law or a rule for every learning tool (reading, sensitive note). Sources: the World Bank working paper and the PNAS paper replace the two blog and news reports (UN News, World Bank blog; the Wharton report is named in the PNAS label), and UNESCO's catalogue record is added. "Hundreds of millions of people use them" became "Many people use them" (no source checked for the number). Claim record in claims/DW11.md.
